# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was an American computer scientist, electrical engineer, and a pioneering innovator in integrated circuit (VLSI) design. Early in her career at IBM, she invented dynamic instruction scheduling utilized in superscalar architectures but was fired in 1968 after revealing her intention to undergo gender transition. After her transition, Conway rebuilt her career, working at Memorex, Xerox PARC, MIT, DARPA, and ultimately as a professor emerita at the University of Michigan. At Xerox PARC, she co-developed the ground-breaking Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology and founded the multiproject wafer technology, which became foundational for chip design, facilitated by the MOSIS infrastructure. Her textbook "Introduction to VLSI Systems" revolutionized chip design education and practice, enabling rapid prototyping and spurring the growth of the electronic design automation industry and the foundry model for semiconductors.
Conway was also a prominent transgender rights activist, sharing her life story publicly from 1999 onward and providing resources and advocacy for transgender individuals. She coined the "Conway effect" to describe the marginalization of innovators from underrepresented groups. Throughout her life, she received numerous honors, including election to the National Academy of Engineering, the IEEE Computer Pioneer Award, and the National Inventors Hall of Fame. Conway was recognized not only for her technical achievements but also for her contributions to inclusion and diversity within engineering and computer science. She died in June 2024 at the age of 86.
